mcqs.question: In the packages demonstration, which class is used as an example of importing an API package?

options.A: java.util.Scanner
options.B: java.lang.Math with Math.sqrt()
options.C: java.io.BufferedReader
options.D: javax.swing.JFrame

mcqs.explanation: The NPTEL Lecture 19 demonstration uses java.lang.Math (specifically Math.sqrt()) as an example of importing and using an API package. Since java.lang is auto-imported, Math.sqrt() can be used without an explicit import.

mcqs.question: In the demonstration, what user-defined package is created?

options.A: com.nptel.java
options.B: myInterface
options.C: utils.math
options.D: custom.pack

mcqs.explanation: The NPTEL Lecture 19 demonstration creates a user-defined package called 'myInterface'. Classes in this package are stored in a directory named 'myInterface', demonstrating how user-defined packages map to directory structures.

mcqs.question: What import statement is used to access the user-defined package 'myInterface' in the demonstration?

options.A: package myInterface;
options.B: include myInterface.*;
options.C: import myInterface.*;
options.D: use myInterface.*;

mcqs.explanation: 'import myInterface.*;' imports all public classes from the 'myInterface' package, making them available without fully qualified names. This demonstrates the standard import mechanism for user-defined packages.

mcqs.question: What access level must a class have for it to be accessible from outside its package?

options.A: default (no modifier)
options.B: protected
options.C: private
options.D: public

mcqs.explanation: Only public classes are accessible from outside their package. Default (package-private) classes are inaccessible from different packages. In the demonstration, classes in 'myInterface' must be declared public to be used by classes in other packages.

mcqs.question: In the demonstration, what is 'default access' equivalent to in terms of package visibility?

options.A: Accessible from everywhere
options.B: Package-level access — accessible within the same directory/package only
options.C: Accessible only within the class
options.D: Accessible from subclasses only

mcqs.explanation: Default access (no modifier) means package-level access. Classes and members without an access modifier are accessible only from within the same package (same directory). The demonstration shows that a default class becomes inaccessible when accessed from a different package.

mcqs.question: What example value is shown in the lecture for setting CLASSPATH on Windows?

options.A: set CLASSPATH=C:\Windows\System32
options.B: set CLASSPATH=C:\MyPrograms\Java
options.C: set CLASSPATH=%JAVA_HOME%\lib
options.D: set CLASSPATH=.\myInterface

mcqs.explanation: The NPTEL lecture shows 'set CLASSPATH=C:\MyPrograms\Java' as an example of configuring the CLASSPATH environment variable on Windows to tell the JVM where to find user-defined packages.

mcqs.question: Can class inheritance work across packages when using user-defined packages?

options.A: No — inheritance only works within the same package
options.B: Yes — a class in one package can extend a public class from another package
options.C: Only with protected access modifier
options.D: Only for abstract classes

mcqs.explanation: Class inheritance works across packages. A class in 'com.app' can extend a public class from 'myInterface' package using 'extends' after importing the class. This is demonstrated in the lecture — the demonstration shows inheritance across the imported user-defined package.

mcqs.question: When is CLASSPATH setting needed?

options.A: Always — CLASSPATH must be set for any Java program to run
options.B: Only when packages are located outside the current working directory
options.C: Only when using multiple classes
options.D: Only for applet programs

mcqs.explanation: CLASSPATH is needed when class files or packages are in directories other than the current working directory. By default, the JVM looks in the current directory. If packages are stored elsewhere (like C:\MyLib), CLASSPATH must be set to include those locations.

mcqs.question: What does the demonstration show about public class accessibility from different packages?

options.A: Public classes are accessible only within their package
options.B: Public classes in a package are accessible from any other package after importing
options.C: Public classes require explicit permission from the package owner
options.D: Public classes are accessible only through inheritance

mcqs.explanation: The demonstration shows that public classes in a user-defined package (like 'myInterface') are accessible from any other package once the package is imported with 'import myInterface.*;'. This is the key visibility rule for cross-package class usage.

mcqs.question: What happens in the demonstration when a default (non-public) class is accessed from a different package?

options.A: It works fine
options.B: A compilation error occurs — default class not accessible from different package
options.C: A runtime exception is thrown
options.D: The class is automatically made public

mcqs.explanation: The demonstration explicitly shows that a class without the 'public' modifier (default access) causes a compilation error when accessed from a different package. The error message indicates the class has package-level access and cannot be accessed from outside.

mcqs.question: In the demonstration, what is the correct sequence to create and use a user-defined package 'myInterface'?

options.A: 1)Create directory, 2)Write class with package statement, 3)Compile, 4)Import and use
options.B: 1)Write class, 2)Compile, 3)The directory is auto-created
options.C: 1)Import, 2)Write class, 3)Compile, 4)Run
options.D: 1)Register package in JVM, 2)Write class, 3)Compile

mcqs.explanation: The correct sequence: 1) Create the directory 'myInterface/', 2) Write the Java class with 'package myInterface;' at the top, 3) Compile with javac (optionally use -d to auto-create the directory), 4) In another class, add 'import myInterface.*;' and use the classes.

mcqs.question: Why does the demonstration use 'import java.lang.Math' as an example of an API package, even though it's redundant?

options.A: To show that java.lang can be imported explicitly even though it's automatic
options.B: java.lang must be imported explicitly in Java 8
options.C: Math.sqrt() requires a special import
options.D: To demonstrate that Math is in java.math, not java.lang

mcqs.explanation: Using 'import java.lang.Math' (or 'import java.lang.*') in the demonstration serves a pedagogical purpose — it shows the import syntax and concept even though java.lang is auto-imported. This helps students understand the general import mechanism before applying it to packages that DO require explicit imports.

mcqs.question: In the demo, when inheriting from a class in 'myInterface' package, what must be added to the current class?

options.A: package myInterface;
options.B: import myInterface.ClassName; (or import myInterface.*;) and then extends ClassName
options.C: CLASSPATH must be set to myInterface
options.D: The class must be in the same directory as myInterface

mcqs.explanation: To extend a class from 'myInterface' package: 1) Import the class: 'import myInterface.ClassName;' 2) Declare inheritance: 'class MyClass extends ClassName { ... }'. The import makes the class name available; 'extends' establishes the inheritance.

mcqs.question: What is the difference between 'import java.lang.*' and 'import java.lang.Math' in effect?

options.A: The wildcard form imports more classes, making the program slower
options.B: Functionally identical for using Math; wildcard imports all java.lang classes (all already auto-imported), so both are effectively no-ops
options.C: The specific form is required for static methods
options.D: The wildcard form is invalid for java.lang

mcqs.explanation: Both are redundant for java.lang since it's auto-imported. For other packages, 'import java.util.*' imports everything in java.util, while 'import java.util.Scanner' imports only Scanner. For runtime behavior, both have no difference — imports only affect compile-time name resolution.

mcqs.question: The demonstration shows that CLASSPATH is needed when the package is 'outside the working directory'. What does 'outside' mean here?

options.A: On a different computer
options.B: In a directory not included in the current CLASSPATH search path
options.C: In a different partition of the hard drive
options.D: Only in network drives

mcqs.explanation: 'Outside the working directory' means the package directory is not at (or under) the current working directory or any existing CLASSPATH entry. The JVM only searches the current directory by default — any other location must be added to CLASSPATH.

mcqs.question: In the demonstration, why is access protection in packages important for library design?

options.A: It prevents users from reading the code
options.B: It controls what is part of the public API (public) vs. internal implementation (default/private), giving library designers control over their interface
options.C: It prevents multiple classes in one package
options.D: It makes code run faster

mcqs.explanation: Access protection in packages separates API from implementation: public classes/methods form the stable interface that external code depends on; package-private classes are internal details that can change freely. This is the key design principle — expose what users need, hide what they don't.

mcqs.question: If 'myInterface' package is stored in 'C:\Programs\myInterface', what CLASSPATH setting allows its use?

options.A: set CLASSPATH=C:\Programs\myInterface
options.B: set CLASSPATH=C:\Programs
options.C: set CLASSPATH=C:\Programs\myInterface\*.class
options.D: set CLASSPATH=myInterface

mcqs.explanation: CLASSPATH should point to the PARENT directory of the package directory, not the package directory itself. Setting 'CLASSPATH=C:\Programs' allows the JVM to find 'myInterface/ClassName.class' because it looks for 'C:\Programs\myInterface\ClassName.class' when resolving 'myInterface.ClassName'.

mcqs.question: The demonstration shows that Math.sqrt() is used from the java.lang package. What does this demonstrate about static methods in packages?

options.A: Static methods require a special import syntax
options.B: Static class methods can be called directly using ClassName.methodName() after the class is accessible (via import or full qualification)
options.C: Static methods cannot be in packages
options.D: Static methods require object creation before use

mcqs.explanation: Math.sqrt() demonstrates that static methods in packaged classes are called with ClassName.methodName() syntax. Once the class is accessible (Math via auto-import in java.lang), its static methods are available directly. No object creation (new Math()) is needed.

mcqs.question: What does the demonstration reveal about what happens when you don't add 'public' to a class in 'myInterface' package?

options.A: The class still compiles and works from other packages
options.B: Compilation succeeds but the class is invisible and inaccessible from outside the package
options.C: A compiler warning is generated
options.D: The JVM automatically promotes it to public

mcqs.explanation: A class without 'public' has default (package-private) access. It compiles successfully within its own package, but when another package tries to use it (after import), the compiler reports an error: 'ClassName is not public in package myInterface; cannot be accessed from outside package'.

mcqs.question: How does the demonstration prove that Java package = directory structure?

options.A: By showing that package declarations are optional
options.B: By showing that the class in 'package myInterface;' must physically be in the 'myInterface/' directory for the JVM to find it
options.C: By showing that multiple packages can share one directory
options.D: By showing that CLASSPATH can override directory structure

mcqs.explanation: The demonstration proves package = directory by showing: a class with 'package myInterface;' MUST be in a directory named 'myInterface/'. When the class file is in the correct directory and CLASSPATH includes the parent directory, the JVM finds it correctly. Moving it to a wrong directory causes class loading failure.

mcqs.question: In the demonstration, if 'myInterface.ClassA' is public but 'myInterface.ClassB' has default access, which can be used from another package?

options.A: Both can be used after importing myInterface.*
options.B: Only ClassA — it's public; ClassB's default access prevents cross-package use
options.C: Only ClassB — default access is more permissive
options.D: Neither can be used from another package

mcqs.explanation: After 'import myInterface.*', only public ClassA is usable from outside the package. ClassB with default access causes a compile error if referenced from another package. The wildcard import makes all public types available, but default-access types remain package-private.

mcqs.question: In the demonstration, inheritance across packages is shown. What specific constraint ensures the inherited class works correctly?

options.A: The parent class must have a no-arg constructor
options.B: The parent class must be public AND the methods to be used must be public or protected
options.C: Both classes must be in the same directory
options.D: The parent class must declare the child class as a friend

mcqs.explanation: For cross-package inheritance to work: 1) The parent class must be public (otherwise it's not accessible from outside the package), and 2) the methods/fields to be inherited and used must be public or protected (private members are inherited but not accessible, default-access members aren't accessible cross-package).

mcqs.question: Why might a production library choose to put all its implementation classes in an '.internal' sub-package?

options.A: For faster compilation
options.B: To visually signal to users that these classes are internal details not meant for external use, even if they are technically public
options.C: The JVM restricts access to .internal packages
options.D: .internal packages are automatically private

mcqs.explanation: Naming internal packages with '.internal' (like org.springframework.internal.*) is a convention that signals to developers: 'these are implementation details, don't use them directly'. While Java doesn't enforce this programmatically (classes may be public for internal use), tools like OSGi and Java modules (module-info.java) can enforce this boundary.

mcqs.question: In the demonstration, 'import myInterface.*' is used. Could you use a specific import 'import myInterface.SpecificClass' instead? What's the tradeoff?

options.A: No — only wildcard imports work for user-defined packages
options.B: Yes — specific import makes dependencies explicit (better for large projects); wildcard is more convenient but obscures which classes are actually used
options.C: Specific imports are only valid for java.* packages
options.D: Wildcard imports are faster at runtime

mcqs.explanation: Both work for user-defined packages. Specific imports (import myInterface.MyClass) make it explicit exactly which classes are used from the package, aiding code readability and refactoring. Wildcard imports are convenient but hide dependencies. Most style guides prefer specific imports for production code.

mcqs.question: The demonstration sets 'CLASSPATH=C:\MyPrograms\Java'. If user types 'java myInterface.MyClass' from C:\Test, what path does the JVM look for?

options.A: C:\Test\myInterface\MyClass.class
options.B: C:\MyPrograms\Java\myInterface\MyClass.class
options.C: C:\MyPrograms\Java\MyClass.class
options.D: Both A and B

mcqs.explanation: The JVM maps the fully qualified class name 'myInterface.MyClass' to a path by replacing dots with directory separators. With CLASSPATH=C:\MyPrograms\Java, it looks for 'C:\MyPrograms\Java\myInterface\MyClass.class'. C:\Test is not in the CLASSPATH (unless '.' is included), so the current directory is not searched.

mcqs.question: What is a 'static import' and how does it differ from a regular import?

options.A: Static import imports static classes only
options.B: Static import (import static ClassName.memberName) allows using static fields/methods without class name prefix: 'sqrt(4)' instead of 'Math.sqrt(4)'
options.C: Static imports are only for java.lang classes
options.D: Static import imports all static methods of all classes in a package

mcqs.explanation: Static import (import static java.lang.Math.*;) allows using static members directly without the class name: 'sqrt(4)' instead of 'Math.sqrt(4)'. Regular import makes class names available without package prefix. Static import is useful for constants and math functions but can reduce readability if overused.

mcqs.question: If the demonstration creates a class in 'myInterface' package that uses another class also in 'myInterface', does it need an import?

options.A: Yes — always need import
options.B: No — classes in the same package can use each other without import
options.C: Only if the classes are in different files
options.D: Only if one class extends the other

mcqs.explanation: Classes in the same package have automatic access to each other without any import statement. 'myInterface.ClassA' can directly reference 'myInterface.ClassB' without importing it. This is one of the benefits of organizing related classes in the same package.

mcqs.question: What is the significance of showing Math.sqrt() in the packages demo when java.lang is auto-imported?

options.A: Math.sqrt() is not in java.lang
options.B: It demonstrates the concept of using classes from packages, establishing the pattern before showing user-defined packages that DO require explicit imports
options.C: Math.sqrt() requires special activation
options.D: It demonstrates that java.lang can be overridden

mcqs.explanation: Using Math.sqrt() (from auto-imported java.lang) serves as a simple, familiar example to establish the concept of 'using a class from a package' before demonstrating user-defined packages. The pedagogical progression: familiar API package → user-defined package, building understanding incrementally.

mcqs.question: Why does Java require packages to mirror directory structure rather than using a separate mapping file?

options.A: Historical accident from the initial Java design
options.B: Directory-to-package mapping is predictable and efficient — the JVM can locate any class directly from its fully qualified name without reading a mapping index
options.C: Operating systems require directories to match class names
options.D: It reduces the size of compiled .class files

mcqs.explanation: The directory-mirrors-package approach enables O(1) class lookup: given 'com.bank.Account', the JVM constructs the path 'com/bank/Account.class' and reads it directly. A mapping file would require reading and parsing an index file first. This design choice makes class loading fast and predictable.

mcqs.question: The demonstration shows class inheritance across packages. What happens to the protected members of the parent class in this cross-package inheritance scenario?

options.A: Protected members become public in the subclass
options.B: Protected members are accessible in the subclass through the subclass's own reference (this), but not through superclass-type references from outside
options.C: Protected members become private in the subclass
options.D: Protected members are inaccessible in cross-package inheritance

mcqs.explanation: In cross-package inheritance, protected members are accessible inside the subclass through 'this' reference or the subclass type. However, Java restricts cross-package protected access: from outside the subclass's package, you cannot access the protected member through a superclass-type reference, only through the subclass type.
